captions.text: All right, I’m looking at the shared notes on projectile motion with the setup and Newton’s law split into horizontal and vertical components. Ready when you want to walk through it.
Why is the horizontal acceleration zero in equation one?

Because we're assuming no horizontal forces — no air resistance, just gravity acting downward. So the horizontal component of Newton’s second law is simply m times x double dot equals zero, which means the horizontal acceleration is zero.
What would it take to make it non-zero?
You’d need a horizontal force — like air drag, wind, or a push from a rocket. Any nonzero horizontal force makes m times x double dot nonzero, so the horizontal acceleration shows up.
The notes say the two directions are uncoupled. What does that actually mean here?

It means the x and y motions don’t affect each other. Gravity only shows up in the y equation, and there’s no x term in it. So you can solve for the horizontal motion without worrying about the vertical, and you handle the vertical separately. They’re independent because there’s no force linking them in this ideal model.
Would that still hold with air resistance?
Would that still hold with air resistance?
Not usually. With air resistance, the drag force depends on the velocity, which has both x and y parts, so the equations get coupled.

No. With air resistance, the force depends on the velocity, which has both horizontal and vertical components. That couples the equations, so you can't treat x and y separately in the clean way we do here.
